requirement_groups.source_instruction: The Major in Logic and Computation Patrick Doyle, Senior Academic Program Manager Location: Baker Hall 161G pdoyle2@andrew.cmu.edu https://go.oncehub.com/PatDoyle Overview The Bachelor of Science in Logic and Computation curriculum is flexible in that it permits students to focus on any of a number of areas including (but not limited to): computer science, artificial intelligence and cognitive science, logic and the foundations of mathematics, methodology and philosophy of science. Curriculum The Logic and Computation major requires 13 courses and a senior thesis. Students in their first and sophomore year, are expected to complete the five courses in Introduction to Formal Systems, which include courses in mathematics, statistics, computer science and philosophy. Students must then complete the Logic Core which includes 80-310 Formal Logic and 80-311 Undecidability and Incompleteness . These courses provide comprehensive background in logic, computability, and analytic philosophy. In addition students will take two courses in the Computer Science core which introduce students to imperative computation and functional programming. Four advanced electives are chosen in the area of focus, as described below in the sample curricula, and should support independent research towards fulfilling the senior thesis requirement. In their senior year, Primary and Additional Majors in Logic and Computation will engage in original research under the supervision of a faculty advisor in 80-595 Senior Thesis (a workload equivalent of 12 units). Students are responsible for identifying a thesis topic and securing a faculty advisor prior to the start of the semester in which they plan to complete the thesis. Note: Students should work with the Senior Academic Program Manager during their junior year to begin the process of identifying their topic and potential advisors. All courses, if taken at Carnegie Mellon University, must be taken for a letter grade and passed with a grade of "C" or above. Students may double count any course for the major with another major or minor. No more than two courses transferred from another institution may count towards the major requirements. Core Courses Introduction to Formal Systems 51 units
